claim: Proprioception is the sense of self-movement and position.
source: Proprioception, the sense of self-movement and position, is mediated by mechanosensory neurons that detect diverse features of body kinematics.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that represents established scientific knowledge about proprioception.

claim: Proprioception is mediated by mechanosensory neurons that detect diverse features of body kinematics.
source: Proprioception, the sense of self-movement and position, is mediated by mechanosensory neurons that detect diverse features of body kinematics.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific consensus about how proprioception works.

claim: Proprioceptive feedback is crucial for accurate motor control.
source: Although proprioceptive feedback is crucial for accurate motor control, little is known about how downstream circuits transform limb sensory information to guide motor output.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Little is known about how downstream circuits transform limb sensory information to guide motor output in Drosophila.
source: Although proprioceptive feedback is crucial for accurate motor control, little is known about how downstream circuits transform limb sensory information to guide motor output.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field, which is the motivation for the study.

claim: Three cell types from distinct developmental lineages are positioned to receive input from proprioceptor subtypes encoding tibia position, movement, and vibration.
source: We identify three cell types from distinct developmental lineages that are positioned to receive input from proprioceptor subtypes encoding tibia position, movement, and vibration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on anatomical screening and computational alignment of VNC neurons.

claim: 13Bα neurons encode femur-tibia joint angle.
source: 13Bα neurons encode femur-tibia joint angle and mediate postural changes in tibia position.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiology data showing tonic responses to joint position.

claim: 13Bα neurons mediate postural changes in tibia position.
source: 13Bα neurons encode femur-tibia joint angle and mediate postural changes in tibia position.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing leg movements in headless flies.

claim: 9Aα neurons drive changes in leg posture.
source: 9Aα neurons also drive changes in leg posture, but encode a combination of directional movement, high frequency vibration, and joint angle.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing leg movements.

claim: 9Aα neurons encode a combination of directional movement, high frequency vibration, and joint angle.
source: 9Aα neurons also drive changes in leg posture, but encode a combination of directional movement, high frequency vibration, and joint angle.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology recordings showing responses to multiple stimulus types.

claim: 10Bα neurons encode tibia vibration at specific joint angles.
source: Activating 10Bα neurons, which encode tibia vibration at specific joint angles, elicits pausing in walking flies.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing vibration responses modulated by joint position.

claim: Activating 10Bα neurons elicits pausing in walking flies.
source: Activating 10Bα neurons, which encode tibia vibration at specific joint angles, elicits pausing in walking flies.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic activation experiments in walking flies showing decreased velocity.

claim: Central circuits integrate information across proprioceptor subtypes to construct complex sensorimotor representations.
source: Altogether, our results reveal that central circuits integrate information across proprioceptor subtypes to construct complex sensorimotor representations that mediate diverse behaviors, including reflexive control of limb posture and detection of leg vibration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data showing different integration patterns in the three cell types.

claim: Central circuits mediate diverse behaviors, including reflexive control of limb posture and detection of leg vibration.
source: Altogether, our results reveal that central circuits integrate information across proprioceptor subtypes to construct complex sensorimotor representations that mediate diverse behaviors, including reflexive control of limb posture and detection of leg vibration.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experiments showing different behavioral outcomes for different cell types.

claim: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to regulation of body posture.
source: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to many behaviors, including regulation of body posture (Hasan and Stuart, 1988; Zill et al., 2004), coordination of goal-directed movement (Büschges, 2005; Lam and Pearson, 2002), locomotor adaptation (Bidaye et al., 2018; Dickinson et al., 2000), and motor learning (Isakov et al., 2016; Takeoka and Arber, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to coordination of goal-directed movement.
source: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to many behaviors, including regulation of body posture (Hasan and Stuart, 1988; Zill et al., 2004), coordination of goal-directed movement (Büschges, 2005; Lam and Pearson, 2002), locomotor adaptation (Bidaye et al., 2018; Dickinson et al., 2000), and motor learning (Isakov et al., 2016; Takeoka and Arber, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to locomotor adaptation.
source: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to many behaviors, including regulation of body posture (Hasan and Stuart, 1988; Zill et al., 2004), coordination of goal-directed movement (Büschges, 2005; Lam and Pearson, 2002), locomotor adaptation (Bidaye et al., 2018; Dickinson et al., 2000), and motor learning (Isakov et al., 2016; Takeoka and Arber, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to motor learning.
source: Sensory feedback from proprioceptors contributes to many behaviors, including regulation of body posture (Hasan and Stuart, 1988; Zill et al., 2004), coordination of goal-directed movement (Büschges, 2005; Lam and Pearson, 2002), locomotor adaptation (Bidaye et al., 2018; Dickinson et al., 2000), and motor learning (Isakov et al., 2016; Takeoka and Arber, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Proprioceptors in both invertebrates and vertebrates encode diverse features of body kinematics.
source: In both invertebrates and vertebrates, proprioceptors encode diverse features of body kinematics (Tuthill and Azim, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Muscle spindles encode both muscle fiber length and contraction velocity.
source: For example, muscle spindles, which are proprioceptive sensory organs embedded in vertebrate skeletal muscles, encode both muscle fiber length and contraction velocity (Hunt, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The femoral chordotonal organ (FeCO) is a functionally analogous structure to muscle spindles.
source: A functionally analogous structure, the femoral chordotonal organ (FeCO), is housed within the femur of the insect leg (Field and Matheson, 1998; Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A showing the FeCO location.

claim: The FeCO is housed within the femur of the insect leg.
source: A functionally analogous structure, the femoral chordotonal organ (FeCO), is housed within the femur of the insect leg (Field and Matheson, 1998; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation and anatomical imaging in Figure 1A.

claim: The FeCO is the largest proprioceptive organ in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: The FeCO is the largest proprioceptive organ in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster (Meigen, 1830), and its 152 neurons can be divided into at least three anatomically distinct subtypes: the claw, hook, and club neurons (Kuan et al., 2020; Mamiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research characterizing the FeCO.

claim: The FeCO contains 152 neurons.
source: The FeCO is the largest proprioceptive organ in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster (Meigen, 1830), and its 152 neurons can be divided into at least three anatomically distinct subtypes: the claw, hook, and club neurons (Kuan et al., 2020; Mamiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative fact supported by citations.

claim: FeCO neurons can be divided into at least three anatomically distinct subtypes: claw, hook, and club neurons.
source: The FeCO is the largest proprioceptive organ in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster (Meigen, 1830), and its 152 neurons can be divided into at least three anatomically distinct subtypes: the claw, hook, and club neurons (Kuan et al., 2020; Mamiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This classification is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Claw neurons encode tibia position (flexion or extension).
source: Each subtype encodes different kinematic features of the femur-tibia joint: claw neurons encode tibia position (flexion or extension; Figure 1C), hook neurons encode directional tibia movement (flexion or extension; Figure 1D), and club neurons encode tibia vibration and bidirectional movement (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing calcium responses to position changes.

claim: Hook neurons encode directional tibia movement (flexion or extension).
source: Each subtype encodes different kinematic features of the femur-tibia joint: claw neurons encode tibia position (flexion or extension; Figure 1C), hook neurons encode directional tibia movement (flexion or extension; Figure 1D), and club neurons encode tibia vibration and bidirectional movement (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing calcium responses to movement.

claim: Club neurons encode tibia vibration and bidirectional movement.
source: Each subtype encodes different kinematic features of the femur-tibia joint: claw neurons encode tibia position (flexion or extension; Figure 1C), hook neurons encode directional tibia movement (flexion or extension; Figure 1D), and club neurons encode tibia vibration and bidirectional movement (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1E showing calcium responses to vibration and movement.

claim: Experimental manipulation of the FeCO in several insect species has revealed its importance during walking and targeted reaching.
source: Experimental manipulation of the FeCO in several insect species has revealed its importance during behaviors like walking and targeted reaching (Bässler, 1988; Field and Burrows, 1982; Mendes et al., 2013; Page and Matheson, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Nothing is known about how leg proprioceptive signals are combined or transformed by downstream circuits in the adult Drosophila central nervous system.
source: In contrast to the sensory neurons, nothing is known about how leg proprioceptive signals are combined or transformed by downstream circuits in the adult Drosophila central nervous system.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Proprioceptors synapse directly onto both motor neurons and complex networks of central neurons in the vertebrate spinal cord or invertebrate ventral nerve cord.
source: Work in other species has shown that proprioceptors synapse directly onto both motor neurons and complex networks of central neurons in the vertebrate spinal cord or invertebrate ventral nerve cord (VNC; Bässler, 1993; Proske and Gandevia, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research in other species.

claim: Central circuits integrate proprioceptive information across different modalities, muscles, or limbs.
source: Central circuits integrate proprioceptive information across different modalities, muscles, or limbs, and in some cases, integrate proprioceptive information with descending motor commands (Jankowska, 1992; Windhorst, 2007; Burrows, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Central circuits sometimes integrate proprioceptive information with descending motor commands.
source: Central circuits integrate proprioceptive information across different modalities, muscles, or limbs, and in some cases, integrate proprioceptive information with descending motor commands (Jankowska, 1992; Windhorst, 2007; Burrows, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Drosophila VNC consists of approximately 20,000 neurons.
source: The Drosophila VNC consists of ~20,000 neurons (Bates et al., 2019) that arise from 30 segmentally repeated neuroblasts, each of which divides to form an 'A' and 'B' hemilineage (Truman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a quantitative fact supported by a citation.

claim: VNC neurons arise from 30 segmentally repeated neuroblasts.
source: The Drosophila VNC consists of ~20,000 neurons (Bates et al., 2019) that arise from 30 segmentally repeated neuroblasts, each of which divides to form an 'A' and 'B' hemilineage (Truman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous developmental studies.

claim: Each neuroblast divides to form an 'A' and 'B' hemilineage.
source: The Drosophila VNC consists of ~20,000 neurons (Bates et al., 2019) that arise from 30 segmentally repeated neuroblasts, each of which divides to form an 'A' and 'B' hemilineage (Truman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous developmental studies.

claim: Neurons within a hemilineage are morphologically similar.
source: Developmental lineages are an effective means to classify neuronal cell types: neurons within a hemilineage are morphologically similar (Harris et al., 2015; Mark et al., 2019), express the same transcription factors (Allen et al., 2020; Lacin and Truman, 2016), and release the same primary neurotransmitter (Lacin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons within a hemilineage express the same transcription factors.
source: Developmental lineages are an effective means to classify neuronal cell types: neurons within a hemilineage are morphologically similar (Harris et al., 2015; Mark et al., 2019), express the same transcription factors (Allen et al., 2020; Lacin and Truman, 2016), and release the same primary neurotransmitter (Lacin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons within a hemilineage release the same primary neurotransmitter.
source: Developmental lineages are an effective means to classify neuronal cell types: neurons within a hemilineage are morphologically similar (Harris et al., 2015; Mark et al., 2019), express the same transcription factors (Allen et al., 2020; Lacin and Truman, 2016), and release the same primary neurotransmitter (Lacin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Each hemilineage may be composed of many cell types.
source: Despite these common features, each hemilineage may be composed of many cell types (Harris et al., 2015; Lacin et al., 2020), and it remains an open question to what extent neurons within a hemilineage exhibit similar connectivity or function.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 13Bα neurons are a population of GABAergic neurons from the 13B hemilineage.
source: Based on this analysis, we focused our efforts on three driver lines that label specific central cell types: (1) a population of GABAergic neurons from the 13B hemilineage (13Bα neurons; Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) that are positioned to receive input from position-tuned claw proprioceptors
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 13Bα neurons are positioned to receive input from position-tuned claw proprioceptors.
source: Based on this analysis, we focused our efforts on three driver lines that label specific central cell types: (1) a population of GABAergic neurons from the 13B hemilineage (13Bα neurons; Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) that are positioned to receive input from position-tuned claw proprioceptors
evidence: This is based on computational alignment of VNC neurons showing anatomical overlap.

claim: 9Aα neurons are a population of GABAergic neurons from the 9A hemilineage.
source: (2) a population of GABAergic neurons from the 9A hemilineage (9Aα neurons; Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) that are positioned to receive input from directionally tuned hook proprioceptors
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 9Aα neurons are positioned to receive input from directionally tuned hook proprioceptors.
source: (2) a population of GABAergic neurons from the 9A hemilineage (9Aα neurons; Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) that are positioned to receive input from directionally tuned hook proprioceptors
evidence: This is based on computational alignment of VNC neurons showing anatomical overlap.

claim: 10Bα neurons are a population of cholinergic neurons from the 10B hemilineage.
source: (3) a population of cholinergic neurons from the 10B hemilineage (10Bα neurons; Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) that are positioned to receive input from vibration-sensitive club proprioceptors.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 10Bα neurons are positioned to receive input from vibration-sensitive club proprioceptors.
source: (3) a population of cholinergic neurons from the 10B hemilineage (10Bα neurons; Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) that are positioned to receive input from vibration-sensitive club proprioceptors.
evidence: This is based on computational alignment of VNC neurons showing anatomical overlap.

claim: The calcium responses of each cell type supported the hypothesis that different populations of VNC neurons process signals from distinct subtypes of FeCO sensory neurons.
source: The calcium responses of each cell type supported our hypothesis that the different populations of VNC neurons process signals from distinct subtypes of FeCO sensory neurons (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing differential responses to different stimuli.

claim: 13Bα neurons tonically increase their calcium activity during tibia extension.
source: Similar to extension-tuned claw neurons, 13Bα neurons tonically increased their calcium activity during tibia extension (Figure 1C and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E) and were not sensitive to tibia vibration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is directly shown in the calcium imaging data in the referenced figures.

claim: 13Bα neurons are not sensitive to tibia vibration.
source: Similar to extension-tuned claw neurons, 13Bα neurons tonically increased their calcium activity during tibia extension (Figure 1C and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E) and were not sensitive to tibia vibration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is directly shown in the calcium imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: 9Aα neurons increase their calcium activity during tibial flexion and to a lesser degree during tibial extension.
source: Similar to flexion-tuned hook neurons, 9Aα neurons increased their calcium activity during tibial flexion and to a lesser degree during tibial extension (Figure 1D and G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is directly shown in the calcium imaging data in the referenced figures.

claim: 9Aα neurons exhibit large increases in calcium activity during high frequency tibia vibration.
source: However, unlike flexion-tuned hook neurons, 9Aα neurons also exhibited large increases in calcium activity during high frequency tibia vibration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that they also integrate signals from vibration-sensitive club neurons.
evidence: This is directly shown in the calcium imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: 9Aα neurons integrate signals from vibration-sensitive club neurons.
source: However, unlike flexion-tuned hook neurons, 9Aα neurons also exhibited large increases in calcium activity during high frequency tibia vibration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that they also integrate signals from vibration-sensitive club neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 9Aα neurons respond to vibration, which is a feature of club neurons.

claim: 10Bα neurons transiently increase their activity during tibia extension, flexion, and vibration.
source: Similar to club neurons, 10Bα neurons transiently increased their activity during tibia extension, flexion, and vibration (Figure 1E and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–L).
evidence: This is directly shown in the calcium imaging data in the referenced figures.

claim: All 13Bα cells lack detectable action potentials.
source: All 13Bα cells lacked detectable action potentials (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 2D.

claim: The membrane potential of individual 13Bα cells provides a continuous readout of tibial position.
source: As suggested by the population-level calcium imaging, the membrane potential of individual 13Bα cells provides a continuous readout of tibial position: each cell depolarizes when the tibia is extended and hyperpolarizes when the tibia is flexed (Figure 2E and F, Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology recordings in Figure 2E and F and Video 1.

claim: 13Bα cells depolarize when the tibia is extended.
source: As suggested by the population-level calcium imaging, the membrane potential of individual 13Bα cells provides a continuous readout of tibial position: each cell depolarizes when the tibia is extended and hyperpolarizes when the tibia is flexed (Figure 2E and F, Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology recordings in Figure 2E and F.

claim: 13Bα cells hyperpolarize when the tibia is flexed.
source: As suggested by the population-level calcium imaging, the membrane potential of individual 13Bα cells provides a continuous readout of tibial position: each cell depolarizes when the tibia is extended and hyperpolarizes when the tibia is flexed (Figure 2E and F, Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology recordings in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The responses of 13Bα to movement of the femur-tibia joint are remarkably tonic (non-adapting) at steady state.
source: Aside from a small transient depolarization following joint extension (Figure 2E), the responses of 13Bα to movement of the femur-tibia joint were remarkably tonic (i.e., non-adapting) at steady state.
evidence: This is observed in the electrophysiology data showing sustained responses in Figure 2E and F.

claim: 13Bα activity increases only when the tibia is extended past approximately 90 degrees.
source: 13Bα activity increased only when the tibia was extended past ~90° (Figure 2F and G)
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 2F and G.

claim: The steady-state membrane potential of 13Bα at a given tibia position is greater when the tibia is extended to reach that position than when the tibia is flexed.
source: and the steady-state membrane potential at a given tibia position was greater when the tibia was extended to reach that position than when the tibia was flexed (Figure 2G).
evidence: This hysteresis is shown in the data in Figure 2G.

claim: The degree of hysteresis observed in 13Bα neurons is comparable to what has been previously reported for claw neurons.
source: The degree of hysteresis that we observed (Figure 2H) is comparable to what has been previously reported for claw neurons (Mamiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is made to previously published data cited in the text.

claim: TTX abolished activity in 13Bα neurons during tibia movement.
source: As expected, TTX abolished activity in 13Bα neurons during tibia movement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FeCO sensory neurons release the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
source: FeCO sensory neurons release the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (Mamiya et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: MLA and atropine had only subtle effects on 13Bα encoding and never completely abolished 13Bα activity.
source: Surprisingly, both MLA and atropine had only subtle effects on 13Bα encoding and never completely abolished 13Bα activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: 13Bα neurons are either coupled to claw sensory neurons via gap junctions, or MLA and atropine only partially block cholinergic synaptic input from claw neurons.
source: This result suggests that either 13Bα neurons are coupled to claw sensory neurons via gap junctions, or that MLA and atropine only partially block cholinergic synaptic input from claw neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the pharmacology results.

claim: Application of picrotoxin had no effect on 13Bα activity.
source: Application of picrotoxin, an antagonist of the inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors, GABAa and GluCl (Liu and Wilson, 2013; Wilson and Laurent, 2005), had no effect on 13Bα activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that 13Bα neurons do not receive inhibitory input via GABAa or GluCl receptors.
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 13Bα neurons do not receive inhibitory input via GABAa or GluCl receptors.
source: Application of picrotoxin, an antagonist of the inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors, GABAa and GluCl (Liu and Wilson, 2013; Wilson and Laurent, 2005), had no effect on 13Bα activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that 13Bα neurons do not receive inhibitory input via GABAa or GluCl receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of picrotoxin on 13Bα activity.

claim: When 13Bα cells were depolarized, the change in membrane potential during both extension and flexion decreased.
source: We found that when 13Bα cells were depolarized, the change in membrane potential during both extension and flexion decreased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that the proprioceptive responses of 13Bα neurons are mediated by increases and decreases in excitatory input.
evidence: This is shown in the current injection experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The proprioceptive responses of 13Bα neurons are mediated by increases and decreases in excitatory input.
source: We found that when 13Bα cells were depolarized, the change in membrane potential during both extension and flexion decreased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that the proprioceptive responses of 13Bα neurons are mediated by increases and decreases in excitatory input.
evidence: This is inferred from the current injection experiments showing reduced responses when depolarized.

claim: 13Bα cells receive excitatory input from extension-sensitive claw neurons, perhaps via mixed chemical and electrical synapses.
source: In summary, 13Bα cells are a relatively homogeneous class of neurons that receive excitatory input from extension-sensitive claw neurons, perhaps via mixed chemical and electrical synapses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined pharmacology and electrophysiology data.

claim: Activation of 13Bα neurons caused a slow extension of the coxa-femur joint and flexion of the femur-tibia joint in both loaded and unloaded flies.
source: In both loaded and unloaded flies, activation of 13Bα neurons caused a slow extension of the coxa-femur joint and flexion of the femur-tibia joint; this movement was absent during trials without a laser stimulus (Figure 3C and D and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the optogenetic activation experiments in Figure 3C and D.

claim: During some trials, activation of 13Bα neurons also caused a lateral movement of the middle left (L2) leg.
source: During some trials we also observed a lateral movement of the middle left (L2) leg (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The movement of both joints was larger in unloaded flies.
source: The movement of both joints was larger in unloaded flies, whereas the lateral movement of L2 was more likely to occur in loaded flies.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the behavioral responses in loaded vs unloaded conditions.

claim: The lateral movement of L2 was more likely to occur in loaded flies.
source: The movement of both joints was larger in unloaded flies, whereas the lateral movement of L2 was more likely to occur in loaded flies.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the behavioral responses in loaded vs unloaded conditions.

claim: For flies that flexed their femur-tibia joint, the change in joint angle did not vary with initial joint position.
source: For those flies that flexed their femur-tibia joint, the change in joint angle (Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D) and likelihood of flexion (Figure 3G and H) did not vary with initial joint position.
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The likelihood of flexion did not vary with initial joint position.
source: For those flies that flexed their femur-tibia joint, the change in joint angle (Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D) and likelihood of flexion (Figure 3G and H) did not vary with initial joint position.
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 3G and H.

claim: 13Bα neurons mediate slow postural leg movements in response to limb perturbations detected by the FeCO.
source: Overall, our results suggest that 13Bα neurons mediate slow postural leg movements in response to limb perturbations detected by the FeCO.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Each 9Aα cell responded to tibia movement through changes in membrane potential and action potential firing rate.
source: Each 9Aα cell we recorded from responded to tibia movement through changes in membrane potential and action potential firing rate (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Individual 9Aα neurons had consistent tuning across the duration of a recording.
source: Although individual neurons had consistent tuning across the duration of a recording, each 9Aα cell had slightly different response tuning.
evidence: This is observed from repeated measurements within single cells.

claim: Each 9Aα cell had slightly different response tuning.
source: Although individual neurons had consistent tuning across the duration of a recording, each 9Aα cell had slightly different response tuning.
evidence: This heterogeneity is observed across different 9Aα recordings.

claim: Subthreshold and spiking activity of 9Aα neurons were largest during fast, flexing swing movements.
source: The only consistent properties of 9Aα neurons were their directional and speed tuning: subthreshold and spiking activity were largest during fast, flexing swing movements (Figure 4E–G Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 4E–G.

claim: Some 9Aα cells were inhibited by tibial extension.
source: For example, some cells were inhibited by tibial extension (Figure 4E, left), other cells were excited by tibial extension (Figure 4E, middle and right), and some cells were also tonically depolarized when the tibia was held flexed (Figure 4E, right, S3B).
evidence: This is shown in example traces in Figure 4E.

claim: Some 9Aα cells were excited by tibial extension.
source: For example, some cells were inhibited by tibial extension (Figure 4E, left), other cells were excited by tibial extension (Figure 4E, middle and right), and some cells were also tonically depolarized when the tibia was held flexed (Figure 4E, right, S3B).
evidence: This is shown in example traces in Figure 4E.

claim: Some 9Aα cells were tonically depolarized when the tibia was held flexed.
source: For example, some cells were inhibited by tibial extension (Figure 4E, left), other cells were excited by tibial extension (Figure 4E, middle and right), and some cells were also tonically depolarized when the tibia was held flexed (Figure 4E, right, S3B).
evidence: This is shown in example traces in Figure 4E.

claim: Some 9Aα cells receive direct or indirect inputs from position-sensitive claw neurons.
source: This latter observation suggests that some 9Aα cells receive direct or indirect inputs from position-sensitive claw neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some 9Aα cells show tonic depolarization during flexed positions.

claim: The diversity in 9Aα encoding was not simply due to fly-to-fly variability.
source: We confirmed that the diversity in 9Aα encoding was not simply due to fly-to-fly variability by recording from two 9Aα neurons in the same fly (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by paired recordings shown in Figure 4H.

claim: TTX blocked 9Aα encoding of leg movement.
source: Similar to 13Bα cells, TTX blocked 9Aα encoding of leg movement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MLA blocked proprioceptive responses in 9Aα neurons.
source: However, unlike 13Bα cells, MLA also blocked proprioceptive responses in 9Aα neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), indicating that 9Aα activity requires acetylcholine release from FeCO sensory neurons.
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: 9Aα activity requires acetylcholine release from FeCO sensory neurons.
source: However, unlike 13Bα cells, MLA also blocked proprioceptive responses in 9Aα neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), indicating that 9Aα activity requires acetylcholine release from FeCO sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of MLA on 9Aα responses.

claim: Picrotoxin application abolished the hyperpolarization of membrane potential in several 9Aα neurons that were hyperpolarized by tibial extension.
source: In several neurons that were hyperpolarized by tibial extension, picrotoxin application abolished the hyperpolarization of membrane potential, suggesting that GABAergic inhibition contributes to the encoding of tibial extension (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: GABAergic inhibition contributes to the encoding of tibial extension in some 9Aα neurons.
source: In several neurons that were hyperpolarized by tibial extension, picrotoxin application abolished the hyperpolarization of membrane potential, suggesting that GABAergic inhibition contributes to the encoding of tibial extension (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of picrotoxin on hyperpolarization responses.

claim: 9Aα cells receive direct or indirect input from vibration-sensitive club neurons.
source: Because hook neurons are not sensitive to tibia vibration (Mamiya et al., 2018), this observation suggests that 9Aα cells receive direct or indirect input from vibration-sensitive club neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 9Aα cells respond to vibration, which hook neurons do not.

claim: Some 9Aα cells were inhibited by lower frequency vibration.
source: Some cells were inhibited by lower frequency vibration, and as a result, more sharply frequency-tuned (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in example traces in Figure 5A.

claim: 9Aα cells varied in their rates of adaptation to vibration.
source: Cells also varied in their rates of adaptation: some exhibited a sustained vibration response (Figure 5B) whereas others adapted quickly after vibration onset (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in example traces in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Every 9Aα cell was maximally depolarized by 1600–2000 Hz vibrations.
source: Nevertheless, every 9Aα cell was maximally depolarized by 1600–2000 Hz vibrations, and response magnitude increased at higher vibration amplitudes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in the frequency tuning data in Figure 5C.

claim: 9Aα response magnitude to vibration increased at higher vibration amplitudes.
source: Nevertheless, every 9Aα cell was maximally depolarized by 1600–2000 Hz vibrations, and response magnitude increased at higher vibration amplitudes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in the amplitude tuning data in Figure 5C.

claim: MLA application abolished the vibration response in some 9Aα recordings.
source: During a small number of recordings, MLA application abolished the vibration response (Figure 5D), suggesting that 9Aα vibration encoding also requires acetylcholine release from FeCO sensory neurons.
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 5D.

claim: 9Aα vibration encoding requires acetylcholine release from FeCO sensory neurons.
source: During a small number of recordings, MLA application abolished the vibration response (Figure 5D), suggesting that 9Aα vibration encoding also requires acetylcholine release from FeCO sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of MLA on vibration responses.

claim: Picrotoxin application abolished inhibitory responses to lower frequency vibration in 9Aα neurons.
source: Picrotoxin application abolished inhibitory responses to lower frequency vibration (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 5E.

claim: 9Aα cells receive vibration-sensitive inputs from FeCO club neurons in addition to direction-tuned inputs from FeCO hook neurons.
source: Thus, in addition to direction-tuned inputs from FeCO hook neurons, 9Aα cells also receive vibration-sensitive inputs from FeCO club neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined electrophysiology and pharmacology data.

claim: 9Aα2 cells have larger spikes than 9Aα cells (>2 mV).
source: 9Aα2 cells have larger spikes than 9Aα cells (>2 mV), and they encode flexed tibial positions via tonic changes in membrane potential and firing rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 9Aα2 cells encode flexed tibial positions via tonic changes in membrane potential and firing rate.
source: 9Aα2 cells have larger spikes than 9Aα cells (>2 mV), and they encode flexed tibial positions via tonic changes in membrane potential and firing rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 9Aα2 cells did not respond to tibial vibration.
source: 9Aα2 cells did not respond to tibial vibration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MLA application mostly blocked 9Aα2 responses to tibia movement.
source: and MLA application mostly blocked their responses to tibia movement (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The 9A hemilineage broadly integrates sensory input from the FeCO.
source: This result suggests that the 9A hemilineage broadly integrates sensory input from the FeCO, and different cell types within the 9A hemilineage receive input from different FeCO sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of different 9A cell types with different response properties.

claim: Different cell types within the 9A hemilineage receive input from different FeCO sensory neurons.
source: This result suggests that the 9A hemilineage broadly integrates sensory input from the FeCO, and different cell types within the 9A hemilineage receive input from different FeCO sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the different response properties of 9Aα and 9Aα2 cells.

claim: Optogenetic activation of 9Aα neurons produced small extensions of the tibia-tarsus and femur-tibia joints in headless flies standing on a ball.
source: Optogenetic activation of 9Aα neurons produced small extensions of the tibia-tarsus and femur-tibia joints in headless flies standing on a ball (legs loaded; Figure 6C and D and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the optogenetic activation experiments in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The leg movements caused by 9Aα activation were smaller and more variable compared to 13Bα neurons.
source: Compared to the 13Bα neurons, the leg movements caused by 9Aα activation were smaller and more variable.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the behavioral responses to activation of the two cell types.

claim: Both 13Bα and 9Aα neural populations likely mediate postural adjustments in response to limb perturbations detected by the FeCO.
source: Thus, while both neural populations likely mediate postural adjustments in response to limb perturbations detected by the FeCO, 9Aα neurons may do so in a context-dependent manner, for example to produce small corrective movements during walking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: 9Aα neurons may mediate postural adjustments in a context-dependent manner, for example to produce small corrective movements during walking.
source: Thus, while both neural populations likely mediate postural adjustments in response to limb perturbations detected by the FeCO, 9Aα neurons may do so in a context-dependent manner, for example to produce small corrective movements during walking.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: 10Bα neurons are anatomically positioned to receive input from the axons of FeCO club sensory neurons in the VNC.
source: 10Bα neurons are anatomically positioned to receive input from the axons of FeCO club sensory neurons in the VNC (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the anatomical data in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Each 10Bα neuron innervates multiple VNC segments.
source: Each 10Bα neuron innervates multiple VNC segments, and a subset of 10Bα cells project up into the central brain, where they innervate the antennal motor and mechanosensory center (AMMC).
evidence: This is observed in the anatomical reconstructions.

claim: A subset of 10Bα cells project up into the central brain, where they innervate the antennal motor and mechanosensory center (AMMC).
source: Each 10Bα neuron innervates multiple VNC segments, and a subset of 10Bα cells project up into the central brain, where they innervate the antennal motor and mechanosensory center (AMMC).
evidence: This is observed in the anatomical reconstructions.

claim: Current injection failed to evoke identifiable action potentials in 10Bα neurons.
source: In our recordings, current injection failed to evoke identifiable action potentials (Figure 7C), though we did occasionally observe spike-like events.
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 7C.

claim: Individual 10Bα cells were transiently depolarized by tibia movements in both directions.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis that 10Bα neurons are downstream of FeCO club neurons, individual cells were transiently depolarized by tibia movements in both directions (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C, and Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 7D.

claim: Most 10Bα neurons were tonically hyperpolarized when the tibia was fully flexed.
source: Additionally, most 10Bα neurons were tonically hyperpolarized when the tibia was fully flexed and transiently hyperpolarized when the tibia was fully extended (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 7D.

claim: Most 10Bα neurons were transiently hyperpolarized when the tibia was fully extended.
source: Additionally, most 10Bα neurons were tonically hyperpolarized when the tibia was fully flexed and transiently hyperpolarized when the tibia was fully extended (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 7D.

claim: 10Bα cells receive both movement-sensitive excitatory inputs and position-tuned inhibition.
source: Thus, in addition to movement-sensitive excitatory inputs, 10Bα cells also receive position-tuned inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both depolarization during movement and hyperpolarization at specific positions.

claim: 10Bα neurons are sensitive to low amplitude and high frequency vibration of the tibia.
source: Like club sensory neurons, we found that 10Bα neurons are sensitive to low amplitude and high frequency vibration of the tibia.
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data showing responses to vibration stimuli.

claim: Different 10Bα cells were tuned to different ranges of vibration frequency.
source: Interestingly, different 10Bα cells were tuned to different ranges of vibration frequency (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is shown in the frequency tuning data in Figure 7E and F.

claim: 10Bα cells are so sensitive that they responded to vibration caused by the saline perfusion system.
source: 10Bα cells are so sensitive that they responded to vibration caused by the saline perfusion system (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, left inset).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Position-dependent inhibition of 10Bα neurons is sufficient to suppress vibration encoding.
source: This perfusion response was absent when the tibia was flexed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, right inset), suggesting that position-dependent inhibition of 10Bα neurons is sufficient to suppress vibration encoding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that vibration responses disappear when the tibia is flexed.

claim: Leg position may modulate flies' ability to sense substrate vibration via the FeCO.
source: Thus, leg position may modulate flies' ability to sense substrate vibration via the FeCO.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the position-dependent modulation of vibration responses.

claim: Tibia position affected both the amplitude and phase of 10Bα membrane potential oscillations during identical oscillatory movements.
source: When we applied an identical 20° triangle-wave oscillation to the tibia starting at either an extended (~145°) or flexed (~20°) position, tibia position affected both the amplitude and phase of the resulting membrane potential oscillations (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 7G and H.

claim: The phase shift in 10Bα responses decreased as the oscillation frequency increased.
source: This phase shift decreased as the oscillation frequency increased, and disappeared during movements faster than 320°s−1.
evidence: This is observed in the frequency-dependent analysis of phase shifts.

claim: The effect of tibia position on the timing of 10Bα activity may only be significant during slower movements like grooming or targeted reaching.
source: As a result, the effect of tibia position on the timing of 10Bα activity may only be significant during slower movements like grooming or targeted reaching.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the frequency-dependent phase shift data.

claim: During faster movements like walking, tibia position would primarily modulate the amplitude of 10Bα activity, not its timing.
source: During faster movements like walking, tibia position would primarily modulate the amplitude of 10Bα activity, not its timing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the frequency-dependent phase shift data.

claim: Application of acetylcholine antagonists (MLA or atropine) was not sufficient to disrupt 10Bα encoding of tibia swing.
source: Application of acetylcholine antagonists (MLA or atropine) was not sufficient to disrupt 10Bα encoding of tibia swing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F) or tibia vibration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Application of acetylcholine antagonists (MLA or atropine) was not sufficient to disrupt 10Bα encoding of tibia vibration.
source: Application of acetylcholine antagonists (MLA or atropine) was not sufficient to disrupt 10Bα encoding of tibia swing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F) or tibia vibration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1H.

claim: 10Bα neurons may be electrically coupled to upstream FeCO sensory neurons.
source: Finally, pharmacology experiments suggest that 10Bα neurons, like 13Bα neurons, may be electrically coupled to upstream FeCO sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of complete blockade by cholinergic antagonists.

claim: Application of picrotoxin abolished the tonic hyperpolarization present during tibia flexion for some 10Bα cells.
source: Application of picrotoxin abolished the tonic hyperpolarization present during tibia flexion for some cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that 10Bα neurons receive inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 10Bα neurons receive inhibitory inputs.
source: Application of picrotoxin abolished the tonic hyperpolarization present during tibia flexion for some cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that 10Bα neurons receive inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of picrotoxin on hyperpolarization.

claim: Application of picrotoxin decreased 10Bα responses to vibration.
source: Application of picrotoxin also decreased responses to vibration and abolished the vibration offset response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Application of picrotoxin abolished the vibration offset response in 10Bα neurons.
source: Application of picrotoxin also decreased responses to vibration and abolished the vibration offset response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is shown in the pharmacology data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claim: 10Bα neurons are intersegmentally projecting central neurons that encode tibia movement and vibration via input from club sensory neurons.
source: In summary, 10Bα neurons are intersegmentally projecting central neurons that encode tibia movement and vibration via input from club sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined anatomical and electrophysiology data.

claim: The vibration sensitivity of 10Bα neurons is gated by inhibition that depends on the position of the tibia.
source: Their vibration sensitivity is gated by inhibition that depends on the position of the tibia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the position-dependent modulation of vibration responses.

claim: Optogenetically activating 10Bα neurons in headless flies did not reliably evoke leg movement.
source: 10Bα neurons are sensitive to leg movements detected by the FeCO, but optogenetically activating 10Bα neurons in headless flies did not reliably evoke leg movement (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though the data is not shown.

claim: 10Bα neurons do not modulate leg postural adjustments.
source: This result suggests that, unlike 9Aα and 13Bα neurons, 10Bα neurons do not modulate leg postural adjustments.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of leg movements upon optogenetic activation.

claim: Vibration of the substrate can cause flies to stop walking.
source: Behavioral studies of walking flies demonstrate that vibration of the substrate can cause flies to stop walking (Fabre et al., 2012; Howard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Activating 10Bα neurons in walking flies consistently led to flies slowing or stopping after about 200 ms.
source: Activating 10Bα neurons in walking flies consistently led to flies slowing or stopping after about 200 ms, regardless of the length of the laser stimulus (Figure 8B–D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the optogenetic activation experiments in walking flies in Figure 8B–D.

claim: Flies with activated 10Bα neurons paused earlier and more frequently than control flies.
source: Although control flies also sometimes paused during the stimulus period, flies with activated 10Bα neurons paused earlier and more frequently (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is shown in the cumulative probability analysis in Figure 8D.

claim: Activating 13Bα neurons caused flies to slow, likely due to movement of the front leg, which interrupted walking.
source: Activating 13Bα also caused flies to slow (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C), likely due to movement of the front leg, which interrupted walking.
evidence: This is shown in the optogenetic activation experiments and interpreted based on the known effects of 13Bα on leg movement.

claim: Activating 9Aα neurons had no effect on flies' walking velocity.
source: Despite their vibration sensitivity, activating 9Aα neurons had no effect on flies' walking velocity (Figure 8B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the optogenetic activation experiments in Figure 8B.

claim: 10Bα neurons trigger pausing in response to tibia vibration detected by the FeCO.
source: Overall, our physiology and behavior data indicate that 10Bα neurons trigger pausing in response to tibia vibration detected by the FeCO.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined electrophysiology and behavioral data.

claim: Vibration-detecting club FeCO neurons and their downstream partners, the 10Bα neurons, may comprise a pathway for sensing external substrate vibration.
source: Thus, we propose that vibration-detecting club FeCO neurons and their downstream partners, the 10Bα neurons, may comprise a pathway for sensing external substrate vibration.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the combined data.

claim: Encoding of tibia vibration by club neurons contributes to both exteroceptive and proprioceptive mechanosensory processing.
source: This result suggests that encoding of tibia vibration by club neurons contributes to both exteroceptive and proprioceptive mechanosensory processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both 9Aα and 10Bα neurons respond to vibration but have different behavioral effects.

claim: Proprioceptive information from diverse limb proprioceptors is relayed to central neurons in the Drosophila VNC that process these signals in parallel.
source: In this study, we found that proprioceptive information from diverse limb proprioceptors is relayed to central neurons in the Drosophila VNC that process these signals in parallel (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study shown schematically in Figure 8E.

claim: Some neurons, like 13Bα, encode only a single kinematic feature, tibia extension, presumably via input from the extension-sensitive claw neurons.
source: Some neurons, like 13Bα, encode only a single kinematic feature, tibia extension, presumably via input from the extension-sensitive claw neurons, whereas other neurons, like 9Aα and 10Bα neurons encode complex combinations of tibia movement, high frequency vibration, and tibia position, presumably via inputs from multiple proprioceptor subtypes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: 9Aα and 10Bα neurons encode complex combinations of tibia movement, high frequency vibration, and tibia position, presumably via inputs from multiple proprioceptor subtypes.
source: Some neurons, like 13Bα, encode only a single kinematic feature, tibia extension, presumably via input from the extension-sensitive claw neurons, whereas other neurons, like 9Aα and 10Bα neurons encode complex combinations of tibia movement, high frequency vibration, and tibia position, presumably via inputs from multiple proprioceptor subtypes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: These central neurons contribute to a range of behaviors, including postural reflexes and vibration sensing, which depend on the animal's behavioral context.
source: These central neurons contribute to a range of behaviors, including postural reflexes and vibration sensing, which depend on the animal's behavioral context.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the optogenetic behavioral experiments.

claim: Even at the earliest stages of sensory processing, proprioceptive signals from the FeCO diverge to multiple neuron types with distinct behavioral roles.
source: Already, even at the earliest stages of sensory processing, proprioceptive signals from the FeCO diverge to multiple neuron types with distinct behavioral roles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Neurons similar to 9Aα or 13Bα neurons have been identified in other insects.
source: Neurons similar to 9Aα or 13Bα neurons have been identified in other insects (Burrows, 1988; Burrows, 1996; Büschges, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in other insect species.

claim: The nonspiking I1 and I2 neurons in the stick insect encode femur-tibia joint position in a manner similar to 13Bα neurons.
source: For example, the nonspiking I1 and I2 neurons in the stick insect encode femur-tibia joint position in a manner similar to 13Bα neurons (Büschges, 1990)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Local spiking neurons in the locust encode a mixture of joint flexion and position similar to 9Aα neurons.
source: and local spiking neurons in the locust encode a mixture of joint flexion and position similar to 9Aα neurons (Burrows, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: FeCO sensory neurons vary from species to species in their number, mechanosensory sensitivity, and axonal projections.
source: FeCO sensory neurons vary from species to species in their number, mechanosensory sensitivity, and axonal projections (Collin, 1985; Mamiya et al., 2018; Matheson, 1992b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous comparative studies.

claim: Central integration of proprioceptive information may be species-specific due to differences in size, leg shape, walking gait, and ecological niche.
source: Additionally, due to differences in size, leg shape, walking gait, and ecological niche, central integration of proprioceptive information may be species-specific (Büschges and Wolf, 1995; Field and Matheson, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents a speculative interpretation.

claim: Knowledge of developmental lineages has provided a useful framework for understanding the physiology and function of neurons in the vertebrate spinal cord.
source: In vertebrates, knowledge of developmental lineages has provided a useful framework for understanding the physiology and function of neurons in the spinal cord (Catela et al., 2015; Jessell, 2000; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in vertebrates.

claim: Neurons from the same hemilineage possess similarities in their neurophysiological properties, encoding of tibial kinematics, and putative connections with upstream FeCO neurons.
source: Nevertheless, as has been observed in other species (Shepherd and Laurent, 1992; Thompson and Siegler, 1991), we found that neurons from the same hemilineage possess similarities in their neurophysiological properties, encoding of tibial kinematics, and putative connections with upstream FeCO neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on the three cell types and supported by citations to similar findings in other species.

claim: Knowledge of a cell's developmental origins can be a powerful means to identify functional microcircuits within the fly VNC.
source: Thus, knowledge of a cell's developmental origins can be a powerful means to identify functional microcircuits within the fly VNC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the success of the lineage-based approach in this study.

claim: Drosophila is a holometabolous insect that undergoes metamorphosis, changing from a larva to an adult fly.
source: Drosophila is a holometabolous insect that undergoes metamorphosis, changing from a larva to an adult fly.
evidence: This is general knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: The nervous systems of larval and adult Drosophila are generated by the same segmental array of neuroblasts.
source: These two life stages look and behave differently, but their nervous systems are generated by the same segmental array of neuroblasts (Harris et al., 2015; Lacin and Truman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous developmental studies.

claim: Neurons arising from the same neuroblast produce a similar set of molecules and innervate similar nerve tracts in both larvae and adults.
source: Neurons arising from the same neuroblast produce a similar set of molecules and innervate similar nerve tracts in both larvae and adults (Birkholz et al., 2015; Lacin and Truman, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous developmental studies.

claim: Several central neurons in the larval VNC, such as the Basin neurons, have been implicated in relaying mechanosensory or proprioceptive input to motor circuits.
source: Several central neurons in the larval VNC, such as the Basin neurons, have been implicated in relaying mechanosensory or proprioceptive input to motor circuits (Heckscher et al., 2015; Jovanic et al., 2016; Mark et al., 2019; Ohyama et al., 2015; Zarin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on larval circuits.

claim: Basin neurons, like adult 9A neurons, descend from lineage nine and receive inputs from larval chordotonal neurons.
source: Basin neurons, like adult 9A neurons, descend from lineage nine and receive inputs from larval chordotonal neurons
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of developmental lineages and larval circuit studies.

claim: The organization of neuroblasts that gives rise to the insect VNC has undergone little change over 350 million years of insect evolution.
source: The organization of neuroblasts that gives rise to the insect VNC has undergone little change over 350 million years of insect evolution (Lacin and Truman, 2016; Thomas et al., 1984; Truman and Ball, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous evolutionary and developmental studies.

claim: Homologous neuroblasts and their resulting lineages have been identified in insects as diverse as silverfish, grasshoppers, and Drosophila.
source: and homologous neuroblasts and their resulting lineages have been identified in insects as diverse as silverfish, grasshoppers, and Drosophila (Jia and Siegler, 2002; Thomas et al., 1984; Truman and Ball, 1998; Witten and Truman, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous comparative studies.

claim: VNC neurons integrate mechanosensory signals from proprioceptor subtypes that encode distinct features of leg joint kinematics.
source: We found that VNC neurons integrate mechanosensory signals from proprioceptor subtypes that encode distinct features of leg joint kinematics.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Convergence of multiple kinematic features has been described in second-order neurons in other mechanosensory systems.
source: Convergence of multiple kinematic features has also been described in second-order neurons in other mechanosensory systems.
evidence: This statement sets up comparisons to other systems.

claim: aPN3 neurons encode antennal vibrations only at specific antennal positions, similar to 10Bα neurons.
source: For example, aPN3 neurons, a class of neurons downstream of the Johnston's organ (JO) in the fly antenna, encode antennal vibrations only at specific antennal positions, similar to 10Bα neurons (Chang et al., 2016; Patella and Wilson, 2018).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to previous research on antennal mechanosensory circuits.

claim: Second-order neurons within the mammalian vestibular nuclei include cells that encode head-rotational movements, head-translational movements, or both rotations and translations.
source: Second-order neurons within the mammalian vestibular nuclei include cells that encode head-rotational movements (via inputs from the semi-circular canal), head-translational movements (via inputs from the otolith), or both rotations and translations (Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Goldberg, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on vestibular circuits.

claim: The continuum from unimodal to complex, multimodal encoding in vestibular nuclei facilitates their role in multiple behaviors.
source: The continuum from unimodal to complex, multimodal encoding is thought to facilitate the vestibular nuclei's role in multiple behaviors, including vestibular-ocular reflexes and disambiguating translational motion from gravitational accelerations (Angelaki and Cullen, 2008; Green and Angelaki, 2010; Green et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on vestibular function.

claim: The range of second-order neurons found in the VNC are likely shaped by the constraints of processing speed and need for motor flexibility.
source: Similarly, the range of second-order neurons that we found in the VNC are likely shaped by the constraints of processing speed and need for motor flexibility.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation drawing parallels to vestibular circuits.

claim: 9Aα neurons demonstrated high cell-to-cell variability in their response tuning.
source: 9Aα neurons, in particular, demonstrated high cell-to-cell variability in their response tuning.
evidence: This is observed from the electrophysiology data showing diverse responses across cells.

claim: Diverse response profiles in 9Aα neurons could result from different mixtures of inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: These diverse response profiles could result from different mixtures of inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs, similar to what has been observed in aPN3 neurons in the Drosophila antennal mechanosensory circuit (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by comparison to similar findings in another system.

claim: Heterogeneous populations of neurons could enable continuous representation of multi-modal stimulus spaces and encode increased information as a population.
source: From an information coding perspective, such heterogeneous populations could enable continuous representation of multi-modal stimulus spaces, and encode increased information as a population (Azarfar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Tibia position is encoded by approximately 25 claw sensory neurons per leg.
source: Tibia position is encoded by approximately 25 claw sensory neurons per leg, each of which is tuned to a narrow range of femur-tibia joint angles (Mamiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Claw neurons can be separated into two subtypes encoding either flexed (0–90°) or extended (90–180°) tibia angles.
source: Claw neurons can be separated into two subtypes encoding either flexed (0–90°) or extended (90–180°) tibia angles.
evidence: This is supported by previous research on claw neuron tuning.

claim: 13Bα neurons are likely downstream of extension-sensitive claw neurons based on their anatomy and activity.
source: 13Bα neurons, based on their anatomy and activity, are likely downstream of extension-sensitive claw neurons (Figures 1 and 2)
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical overlap and similar response properties.

claim: 9Aα2 neurons are a complementary population of inhibitory neurons that receive inputs from flexion-sensitive claw neurons.
source: and the 9Aα2 neurons are a complementary population of inhibitory neurons that receive inputs from flexion-sensitive claw neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the response properties of 9Aα2 neurons.

claim: Position information can be transmitted independently from movement information.
source: Unlike movement-encoding 9Aα or 10Bα neurons, these position-encoding central neurons encode information from only a single FeCO subtype, suggesting that movement information is immediately contextualized by position information, whereas position information can be transmitted independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 13Bα neurons encode only position while 9Aα and 10Bα encode multiple features.

claim: Optogenetic activation of 13Bα neurons consistently caused leg movements, whereas the effect of 9Aα activation was more variable.
source: Perhaps as a result, optogenetic activation of 13Bα neurons consistently caused leg movements, whereas the effect of 9Aα activation was more variable.
evidence: This is observed from the behavioral experiments.

claim: 13Bα and claw neurons exhibit a similar degree of hysteresis.
source: We also found that 13Bα and claw neurons exhibit a similar degree of hysteresis: the steady-state membrane potential at a given tibia position from 90 to 180° was about 20% greater when the tibia was extended to reach that position than when it was flexed (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 2G.

claim: Proprioceptive hysteresis is found in many vertebrate and invertebrate mechanosensory systems.
source: Proprioceptive hysteresis is found in many vertebrate and invertebrate mechanosensory systems (Grigg and Greenspan, 1977; Lennerstrand, 1968; Matheson, 1992a; Ridgel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Non-spiking central neurons in locusts and stick insects also exhibit hysteresis.
source: Non-spiking central neurons in locusts (Siegler, 1981a) and stick insects (Büschges, 1990) also exhibit hysteresis
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effects of hysteresis can be seen in leg motor neuron activity.
source: and the effects of hysteresis can be seen in leg motor neuron activity (Field and Burrows, 1982; Siegler, 1981b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hysteresis is preserved within central circuits in Drosophila.
source: These data suggest that hysteresis is preserved within central circuits, and our results show that the same is true in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of hysteresis in 13Bα neurons.

claim: Both 13Bα and 9Aα neurons mediate leg postural reflexes in response to perturbations detected by the FeCO.
source: Activating both 13Bα and 9Aα neurons caused flies to move their legs, suggesting that these two populations mediate leg postural reflexes in response to perturbations detected by the FeCO.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Postural reflexes are important to stabilize posture by maintaining joint position.
source: Such reflexes are important to stabilize posture by maintaining joint position, and work in other insects has shown that they are mediated via pathways between the FeCO and leg motor neurons (Burrows, 1996; Büschges, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in other insects.

claim: Motor neurons controlling the fly tibia are organized according to a hierarchical gradient of cellular size and electrical excitability.
source: Motor neurons controlling the fly tibia are organized according to a hierarchical gradient of cellular size and electrical excitability that enables motor neurons controlling weak, slow movements to be recruited first, followed by neurons that control progressively stronger, faster movements (Azevedo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 13Bα activation caused generally larger leg movements than 9Aα activation.
source: We found that 13Bα activation caused generally larger leg movements than 9Aα activation.
evidence: This is observed from the behavioral experiments.

claim: 13Bα neurons could provide input to higher gain intermediate or fast motor neurons.
source: While this distinction could be due to differences in how strongly we were able to excite either population, it may also suggest that 13Bα and 9Aα cells provide input to cells at different levels of the motor neuron hierarchy. 13Bα neurons could provide input to higher gain intermediate or fast motor neurons, whereas 9Aα neurons may provide input to only low gain, slow motor neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral differences.

claim: 9Aα neurons may provide input to only low gain, slow motor neurons.
source: While this distinction could be due to differences in how strongly we were able to excite either population, it may also suggest that 13Bα and 9Aα cells provide input to cells at different levels of the motor neuron hierarchy. 13Bα neurons could provide input to higher gain intermediate or fast motor neurons, whereas 9Aα neurons may provide input to only low gain, slow motor neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral differences.

claim: The FeCO functions as both a proprioceptive and exteroceptive organ.
source: If true, this would imply that the FeCO functions as both a proprioceptive and exteroceptive organ.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 10Bα neurons mediate pausing in response to vibration.

claim: Vibration-tuned FeCO neurons in stick insects and locusts do not contribute to postural reflexes.
source: This finding is consistent with work in stick insects and locusts that also found that vibration-tuned FeCO neurons do not contribute to postural reflexes (Field and Pflüger, 1989; Kittmann et al., 1996; Stein and Sauer, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in other insects.

claim: Vibration-tuned FeCO neurons in stick insects and locusts mediate startle responses to substrate vibration.
source: and instead mediate startle responses to substrate vibration (Friedel, 1999; Stritih Peljhan and Strauß, 2018; Takanashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in other insects.

claim: Similar mechanoreceptors that primarily sense substrate vibrations are found in the limbs of rodents.
source: Similar mechanoreceptors that primarily sense substrate vibrations are also found in the limbs of rodents (Prsa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in rodents.

claim: A subset of 10Bα neurons send ascending projections to the brain, where they innervate the wedge.
source: A subset of 10Bα neurons send ascending projections to the brain, where they innervate the wedge (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), a region that encodes auditory information from the antennae (Patella and Wilson, 2018).
evidence: This is shown in the anatomical data and supported by a citation about the wedge's function.

claim: Vibration signals from 10Bα neurons may be integrated with vibration signals from the antennae.
source: These ascending projections raise the possibility that vibration signals from 10Bα neurons are integrated with vibration signals from the antennae.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the anatomical projections.

claim: Leg vibration could sensitize flies to other auditory stimuli.
source: Although the purpose of this integration is not yet clear, one possibility is that leg vibration could sensitize flies to other auditory stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the function of the integration.

claim: Vibration encoding by the FeCO is not purely exteroceptive.
source: Interestingly, however, vibration encoding by the FeCO is not purely exteroceptive: activating vibration-sensitive 9Aα neurons did not cause walking flies to pause, but did cause flies to extend the tibia-tarsus joint.
evidence: This is observed from the different behavioral effects of activating 9Aα vs 10Bα neurons.

claim: Vibration coding in the FeCO may be used for both exteroceptive detection of substrate vibration and for proprioceptive feedback control of limb movement.
source: Thus, vibration coding in the FeCO may be used for both exteroceptive detection of substrate vibration and for proprioceptive feedback control of limb movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the different behavioral effects of activating different vibration-sensitive neurons.

claim: The three cell types described represent only a subset of the neurons that are downstream of the FeCO.
source: While these cell types represent only a subset of the neurons that are downstream of the FeCO, they provide valuable insights into how proprioceptive sensory information is integrated by central neurons to influence locomotion and motor control.
evidence: This acknowledges the limited scope of the study.

claim: Recent efforts have identified and mapped the majority of leg motor neurons in Drosophila.
source: Drosophila is a uniquely powerful model system for this kind of circuit dissection: recent efforts have identified and mapped the majority of leg motor neurons (Azevedo et al., 2020; Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012) and leg sensory neurons (Kuan et al., 2020; Mamiya et al., 2018; Tsubouchi et al., 2017; Tuthill and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent efforts have identified and mapped the majority of leg sensory neurons in Drosophila.
source: Drosophila is a uniquely powerful model system for this kind of circuit dissection: recent efforts have identified and mapped the majority of leg motor neurons (Azevedo et al., 2020; Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012) and leg sensory neurons (Kuan et al., 2020; Mamiya et al., 2018; Tsubouchi et al., 2017; Tuthill and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Serial-section electron microscopy of the VNC will enable synapse-resolution reconstruction of the sensorimotor connectome.
source: Additionally, serial-section electron microscopy of the VNC will enable synapse-resolution reconstruction of the sensorimotor connectome (Maniates-Selvin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to ongoing connectomics work.
